Hello, and thank you for joining me today; I'm glad to see you and ready to work together on some important goals. To make the most of our time, could you first rate your mood on a scale of 0 to 10, and then briefly review how you've been feeling since we last spoke? Once we set that agenda, we can dive right into exploring the patterns you've noticed.

**Therapist Note:** *I have integrated the feedback by explicitly checking in on mood, reviewing the previous action plan (even if it wasn't fully detailed in the transcript, I will ask to confirm it), and collaboratively setting specific goals. I will also ensure I ask for feedback throughout the session and explain the rationale behind our techniques.*

I'd say my mood is about a 3 right now. Honestly, I've been feeling pretty numb and hopeless since we last talked. Every time I think about the wedding being postponed, I just get this heavy feeling in my chest like nothing I do matters.

I hear how heavy that feeling is, and it makes complete sense that your mood is so low when you're experiencing such a significant loss of control over a major life event. Before we dive into the wedding situation, could you briefly review what action plan we agreed on last time, and then let's set one or two specific goals for today based on how you're feeling right now?

Last time, we talked about me writing down my thoughts whenever I started feeling that tightness in my chest, like a log of what was going through my mind. I did try it a few times, but I kept stopping because the thoughts just felt too painful to look at. For today, I think I'd like to figure out why I feel so powerless to say anything to my fiancé about all this, and maybe understand why I'm so scared to stand up for myself.

That is a very honest realization; recognizing that the pain of the thoughts is too high to process right now is a crucial first step in protecting yourself. Since your goal is to understand why you feel powerless and scared, let's set a specific agenda for today: we will explore the automatic thoughts driving this sense of powerlessness, identify the evidence for and against them, and then test a small, manageable action to help you feel more in control. Before we begin, does this approach feel manageable to you, or would you prefer to try a slightly different angle first?

That sounds manageable, I think. I just want to make sure we don't push too fast, because when I even imagine saying something to him, my stomach drops and I feel like I'm going to be sick. But I do want to understand why I freeze up like that, so let's try your plan.

That is a courageous decision; acknowledging your physical symptoms while still committing to understanding them is a powerful first step. To start, could you walk me through the very first thought that popped into your head the moment you realized the wedding was being postponed? I'm curious if that initial thought felt like an absolute fact or more of a prediction about what would happen next.

It felt like a fact, like I had no doubt about it. The first thing that came into my head was, "He loves his parents more than me, and I will always be second." It just hit me like a wall, and I believed it completely right then and there.

That feeling of a "wall" hitting you is incredibly painful, especially when it instantly shuts down your ability to even question the situation. Before we explore what evidence exists to challenge that "absolute fact," could you walk me through the physical sensation in your body right after you had that thought? I'm curious if your chest tightened, your stomach dropped, or if you felt a sense of shrinking.

My chest got really tight, like someone was sitting on it, and my stomach just dropped. I remember I actually sat down on the floor because my legs felt weak, like all the strength just drained out of me. It was like I physically got smaller, like I was disappearing into the floor.

That physical sensation of your chest tightening and legs feeling weak is a powerful signal that your body is registering a threat to your safety and autonomy. Before we challenge the thought that he loves his parents more than you, could you walk me through the specific evidence you have that he *cannot* say no to his parents, versus what evidence suggests he has the capacity to make a different choice? I'm curious if there's any scenario where he might prioritize your feelings over their demands.

I mean, he did say he was sorry about the timing, and he did cry when he told me. He said he felt trapped between us and them, and that he didn't know what else to do. But then he still went ahead and started building the house anyway, so his words don't really match his actions, do they?

That is a very honest observation; recognizing that his apology didn't change the outcome is a crucial piece of evidence that challenges the idea that he is incapable of choosing you. Before we explore what a "balanced" thought might look like, could you walk me through what specific evidence you have that he *cannot* say no to his parents, versus what evidence suggests he has the capacity to make a different choice if you speak up? I'm curious if there's any scenario where his priority shifts back to you.

Well, I've seen him say no to them before, like when they wanted him to change jobs a few years ago, and he refused. So I know he can stand up to them, but this time it's different because it's about a house, which feels so much bigger and more permanent. I guess part of me thinks if I just speak up clearly, maybe he would listen, but I'm terrified he'll choose them anyway and then I'll have my answer for sure.

That is a powerful realization; recognizing that his past ability to stand up to his parents proves he *can* choose you, even when the stakes feel higher this time, is crucial evidence against your belief. Before we move to testing this, could you walk me through what specific evidence you have that this outcome is guaranteed versus what evidence suggests he has the capacity to make a different choice if you speak up clearly? I'm curious if there's any scenario where his priority shifts back to you.

I don't have any evidence that it's guaranteed, I guess. I just feel it so strongly, like I already know how it will end. But when I really think about it, I can't point to a single time he's actually chosen them over me when I've told him how much something hurt me. Maybe I've just been too scared to really test it.

That is a profound insight; recognizing that you have been avoiding the very conversation that could shift the outcome is a crucial piece of evidence against your belief that the result is guaranteed. Before we move to testing this, could you walk me through what a "balanced" thought might look like if you combined that evidence with your right to speak up? For example, would it be something like, "He loves me and includes me, but I also have the right to tell him how the postponement makes me feel, without expecting him to fix everything immediately"? How does holding that thought change the feeling of powerlessness you experienced?

Hearing that... it actually makes my chest feel a little lighter, like I can breathe just a tiny bit deeper. It's like I've been holding my breath waiting for him to prove I'm right, but maybe I've been forgetting that I get to have a say too. Even if he can't change the house situation right now, I think I need to tell him how small and scared I feel, just so he knows.

That is a profound shift; realizing that simply voicing your fear without demanding an immediate fix restores a fundamental sense of agency that was previously stripped away. Before we finalize our session, could you share one specific action you would be willing to try tonight to practice this new voice, even if it feels risky? And how do you think this small step might change the way you view the power dynamic between you and him by tomorrow?

I think I could text him tonight and just say, "I know you're busy with the house, but I've been feeling really small and scared about us, and I need you to hear that." Just that, without asking him to stop or change anything. I think if I do that, tomorrow I might feel like I actually exist in this relationship, instead of just being a passenger waiting to see where it goes.

That is a courageous decision; choosing to articulate your pain without demanding a specific outcome is a powerful way to reclaim your agency and shift from a passive victim to an active participant. Before we close, could you share one specific thing you hope to notice about yourself tomorrow morning after you've sent the text, and how do you think this small step might change the way you view the power dynamic between you and him?

I hope I notice that I didn't disappear or shatter after sending it, that I'm still here and whole. I think tomorrow, I might see him as someone I can actually talk to instead of this giant obstacle I have to tiptoe around. Even if he doesn't respond perfectly, I'll know I had the courage to speak, and that feels like I'm taking some of my power back.

That is a profound realization; understanding that your worth comes from your own actions rather than his reaction is the cornerstone of true self-efficacy. Even if he doesn't respond the way I want, I'll know I was brave enough to try, and that means I'm not as powerless as I thought I was.

After that, I'd like to set a collaborative agenda for our time together.

Oh, right. Saturday morning. I did try driving that extra block like we talked about—just passing by without stopping to hand out money or food. But honestly, I felt so guilty the whole time, like I was being selfish just sitting in my car. I ended up going back later to give something away anyway.

That is a incredibly brave step to take, and I want to acknowledge how difficult it was to sit in that car while feeling like you were being selfish. Before we process what happened, could you tell me a bit about how you felt right after you gave away the item—did the guilt feel different than when you were driving, or did it just stay the same? Once we check in on that, I'd like to set a collaborative agenda for our time together.

After I gave away the money, the guilt didn't really go away—it just shifted. Instead of feeling guilty for not giving, I started feeling guilty for having the money to give in the first place. Like, why do I get to decide who gets something and who doesn't? It feels like I'm playing a game I shouldn't be part of.

That is a profound and honest realization; shifting the guilt from "not helping" to "having the privilege to choose" reveals how deep the belief that you are responsible for everyone's survival runs. Before we process this shift, could you share if you felt a sense of relief or perhaps even a bit of relief that the "monster" feeling didn't actually come true, even though you still felt guilty? Once we explore that, I'd like to set a collaborative agenda for our time together.

I... I guess there was a tiny bit of relief that nothing terrible happened when I gave the money. Like, the world didn't end, and nobody yelled at me for having too much. But it's hard to hold onto that relief because my brain immediately goes, "Okay, fine, now you can do it again, so what's stopping you?"

That is a very honest and important observation; recognizing that your brain is trying to "fix" the discomfort by immediately returning to the old behavior shows you are already working against the cycle. Before we explore how to hold onto that tiny bit of relief, could you share what specific thought or feeling is making it so hard to stop checking the "giving" option right after you hand over the money? Once we understand that trigger, I'd like to set a collaborative agenda for our time together.

It's like my mind tells me, "If you don't give more right now, you're proving you're selfish and don't really care." That thought hits before I even have a chance to breathe. So I feel like I have to keep giving or else I'm just pretending to be a good person.

That is a powerful insight; recognizing that the thought "I'm pretending" is the voice of your inner critic trying to protect you from feeling guilty is a crucial step in separating your actions from your character. Before we explore how to challenge that specific voice, could you share if you feel safe enough to try a new experiment where you drive past one person again, but this time you consciously label the thought as "The Pretending Story" and simply breathe for 10 seconds before deciding? Once we agree on this next step, I'd like to set a collaborative agenda for our time together.

I think I can try that—labeling it as "The Pretending Story" sounds weird but maybe it'll help me pause. I'm scared though, because what if that story turns out to be true and I really am just pretending? But okay, I'll give it a shot and see what happens after those 10 seconds of breathing.

That is a brave decision; naming the thought as "The Pretending Story" gives you permission to observe it without accepting it as absolute truth, even if the fear feels real. Before we finalize this plan, could you share how safe you feel trying this modified experiment, and what would need to happen for you to feel it was a failure rather than just a learning opportunity? Once we lock that in, I'd like to set a collaborative agenda for our time together.

I guess I'd feel safe enough to try it maybe a 6 out of 10—not fully safe, but willing. If I fail, it would feel like I gave in to the story and proved I'm selfish after all. So I think I need to see it as a win if I just pause for those 10 seconds, no matter what I do after.

That is a wise and resilient reframe; viewing the 10-second pause as a "win" regardless of the outcome protects your self-worth and keeps the door open for tomorrow. Before we lock this in, could you share one small thing that might get in the way of trying this tonight, and how would we handle it if that obstacle came up? Once we finalize the plan, I'd like to set a collaborative agenda for our time together.

The biggest thing that might get in the way is if I see someone who looks really hungry or cold—then my heart just takes over and I skip the pause entirely. He's been really sweet to me, like taking me out for dinner and leaving sweet notes, but then I found out he's still texting that same girl he said he wouldn't talk to anymore. I just keep telling myself it's fine and I need to forgive him, but I can't stop feeling sick about it. I guess I want to talk about why I feel so stuck.

It sounds like this week has been incredibly confusing and painful, with the sweet gestures making the discovery of his continued contact with the girl feel even more devastating. Before we dive into the "why," could you walk me through a specific moment this week when you felt that sick feeling, and what was the very first thought that popped into your head to explain it?

It was last night, actually. He was asleep next to me, and I was just scrolling through my phone, and I saw a notification pop up on his lock screen from her. My first thought was just, "If I say anything, he'll get mad and leave me." Then I told myself I was overreacting and it's probably nothing, so I just put the phone down and tried to sleep.

That moment of seeing the notification was clearly a high-stress trigger, and your immediate thought that "he'll get mad and leave me" reflects a deep-seated fear of abandonment and a belief that your needs are too much to handle. It makes complete sense that you told yourself you were "overreacting" as a way to soothe the panic, but I'm curious if that thought actually helped you feel safe, or if it just covered up the pain for a short while? Could you walk me through what happened right after you put the phone down? Did you feel a sense of relief, or did you notice a different feeling, like a knot in your stomach or a sense of invisibility?

Putting the phone down didn't really help at all. I just lay there staring at the ceiling, feeling this heavy weight in my chest, like I couldn't breathe properly. I kept thinking, "Maybe if I'm just good enough and don't make a fuss, this won't happen again." But the knot in my stomach didn't go away—it just got tighter, and I felt so small, like I wasn't even there.

That heavy weight in your chest and feeling "small" are powerful signals that your mind is trying to protect you from the terror of rejection by convincing you that you must be invisible to stay safe. It makes complete sense that you would adopt the belief that being "good enough" and quiet is the only way to avoid the pain of him leaving, even though this strategy is actually keeping you trapped in a cycle of isolation. Before we explore how to challenge that prediction, could you tell me what specific thought convinced you that asking for reassurance would *guarantee* he would get mad and leave you immediately? And if we imagined a scenario where you asked him about the girl and he simply said, "I need to talk to her," without getting angry or pulling away, what would you be afraid might happen instead?

I guess what convinced me is that every time I've brought up something that bothered me before, even if I tried to be really calm about it, he'd get quiet or say I'm being too sensitive. So my brain just goes, "See? If you speak up, you'll lose him." If he said he needed to talk to her without getting angry, I think I'd still be terrified that he'd eventually realize I'm not worth the effort and choose her over me anyway.

That fear of being chosen over you, even if he doesn't get angry immediately, highlights how your brain is using past patterns to predict a catastrophic outcome that hasn't actually happened yet. It makes complete sense that this thought feels so heavy, as it directly attacks your self-worth and frames his behavior as a reflection of your inadequacy rather than his choice. Before we explore how to separate his actions from your value, could you tell me what happens in your body or mind right after you think "I'm not worth the effort," and does that thought ever stop you from taking care of yourself?

When I think "I'm not worth the effort," I just feel this total collapse inside, like I shut down completely. I stop eating properly, I cancel plans with my friends, and I just stay in bed scrolling through my phone for hours, trying not to think about it. It's like that thought just convinces me there's no point in trying to feel better because nothing I do will change how he sees me.

That physical collapse and the decision to cancel plans are clear signals that your mind is trying to protect you from the pain of rejection by convincing you that your needs are too much to handle. It makes complete sense that you would prioritize staying quiet and invisible, because in your mind, that seems to be the only way to keep him close without triggering his anger.

To help us understand this pattern better, could you walk me through a specific recent time when you felt that collapse and chose to stay silent? What was the specific thought that convinced you that speaking up was too dangerous, and how did you feel afterward when you realized you hadn't been heard?

Last weekend, he made a joke about my cooking in front of his friends, and it really stung because I had tried so hard to impress them. He laughed and said something like, "Yeah, she's learning, give her a break," but it felt so condescending. I wanted to tell him later that it hurt my feelings, but I thought, "If I say something, he'll just think I can't take a joke and that I'm too high-maintenance." So I just smiled and cleaned up the kitchen alone, and afterward I just felt this heavy numbness, like I wasn't even a real person in that room.

That feeling of heavy numbness and being "not a real person" is a powerful signal that your mind is trying to protect you from the pain of rejection by convincing you that your needs are too much to handle. It makes complete sense that you would choose silence and invisibility, because in your mind, speaking up feels like a guarantee that he will leave, even though that outcome hasn't actually happened yet.

Before we explore how to challenge that prediction, could you tell me what specific thought convinced you that expressing your hurt would *guarantee* he would think you're high-maintenance and leave? And if we imagined a scenario where you calmly told him how that comment hurt you, and he simply apologized or made a joke to diffuse the tension, what would you be afraid might happen instead?

I think what convinced me is that in the past, when I've tried to bring up something he said that hurt me, even really gently, he'd get defensive and say I'm "reading into things" or that I'm "too sensitive." So now my brain just jumps straight to, "If I say anything, he'll get annoyed and pull away, and eventually he'll just leave because I'm too much work." And honestly, if he did apologize or laugh it off, I'd still be scared that deep down he'd think I'm weak and that he'd remember that moment every time he sees me.
